Figure 1. Proposed Heartverse framework for developmental physiology-guided ECG augmentation and pediatric arrhythmia detection.

(A) Study design. Pediatric ECGs are standardized, and patients are separated into training, validation, and test groups before recordings are divided into segments. Adult-to-child transfer is examined as a supporting study. Generator A uses age information, while generator B also uses knowledge of how the heart changes during development and physiological simulation. Both generators use the same real training patients, model architecture, and training budget. The same classifier architecture is trained separately using real ECGs only, real ECGs plus samples from A, or real ECGs plus samples from B. Standard data augmentation is included for comparison.

(B) ECG generation. Both generators use exact age, rhythm labels, and the same patient information. Generator B additionally uses normal training ECGs and published age references to guide simulation while preserving the intended abnormal rhythm. Synthetic ECGs are added either according to a preset age–rhythm mix or to groups where the model makes more errors. These difficult groups are identified using validation within the training data. Within each strategy, A and B generate the same number of ECGs with the same age–rhythm mix.

(C) Evaluation. Performance will be measured separately by age group and rhythm using real patients kept out of training and model adjustment. Every step that uses pediatric labels will follow the same label budget. We will also examine how the models could prioritize ECGs for review, measuring missed cases, false alarms, and review workload. This analysis will use the actual proportion of positive cases in the test data and decision thresholds chosen using validation data.

Ages 1-16 years are the proposed scope; final age coverage and group boundaries depend on available patients and reliable rhythm labels. Exact age guides generation, while age groups summarize evaluation; axis ticks indicate age values rather than fixed group boundaries. The figure depicts a proposed study, and its signals, distributions and model blocks are schematic rather than empirical results. Demonstrating clinical decision benefit requires a clinician reader study or prospective evaluation.
